items.prompt: Two `setTimeout(..., 0)` callbacks are due in the same tick; the first one (B) queues a promise handler (C), the second logs D. Why is the output B, C, D rather than B, D, C?
items.answer: The microtask queue is drained after each individual macrotask callback, so C runs at the checkpoint between the two timer callbacks
distractors: Timers registered in the same tick are merged into one callback, and promise handlers run inside it in source order
The timers phase is paused whenever a promise is created, and resumes only once that promise settles
C was registered before D in the source file, and every queue is ordered by source position
items.explanation: Microtasks are drained after each macrotask callback, not after the whole phase: two timers due together are still two callbacks with a full checkpoint between them.

items.prompt: `async function buildReport() { const rows = crunch(200000); await save(rows); }` is called from a request handler, and the server freezes while it runs. A teammate says "it's async, it can't block". What is wrong with that claim?
items.answer: Everything before the first await runs synchronously at the call site, so crunch() occupies the stack; only the continuation after await is deferred
distractors: The `async` keyword moves the whole body onto a worker thread, so the freeze must come from save() instead
Async functions are queued as macrotasks, so crunch() waits behind every pending timer before it starts
The body is deferred to the microtask queue, so the freeze comes from a microtask backlog, not from crunch()
items.explanation: await desugars to 'return a promise now and register the rest as a .then handler'; an async function doing expensive work before its first await blocks the caller completely.

items.prompt: The same eight lines print nextTick callbacks before promise callbacks as `.cjs` but after them as `.mjs`. What explains the flip, and which ordering rule should you rely on?
items.answer: An ES module's top level is evaluated inside a promise job, so the microtask drain is already running; rely on the order inside a callback, which is the same in both
distractors: ES modules disable process.nextTick until the module graph finishes loading; rely on queueMicrotask always running first
Node runs .mjs files in a separate event loop with its own queues; rely on nextTick always beating promises
The .mjs loader sorts top-level callbacks alphabetically by queue name; rely on promises always beating nextTick
items.explanation: Module evaluation is a promise job, so top-level microtasks keep draining before the loop returns to the nextTick checkpoint. Inside a callback: nextTick drains, then microtasks, in both module systems.

items.prompt: At the top level of a CommonJS file, `setTimeout(f, 0)` vs `setImmediate(g)` order varies run to run. Inside an `fs.readFile` callback, g always runs before f. Why?
items.answer: The I/O callback runs in the poll phase, and check (setImmediate) is the very next phase; timers only come round on the next loop iteration
distractors: Inside I/O callbacks Node clamps setTimeout to 4 ms, so the immediate always finishes first
readFile callbacks run on the libuv thread pool, where setImmediate is executed synchronously
setImmediate is a microtask while setTimeout is a macrotask, so the immediate wins whenever both are queued together
items.explanation: You are already in the poll phase, so check is next; 'run right after the current I/O, before any timers' is why setImmediate exists. At top level the 1 ms clamp races process startup.

items.prompt: A long CPU loop is chunked, with `await Promise.resolve()` between chunks so that timers and incoming requests get a turn. They still starve. Why, and what should the yield be?
items.answer: The microtask queue drains to empty before the loop advances, so that await never lets the loop move; yield to a macrotask with `await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r))`
distractors: Promise.resolve() is cached after the first call, so later awaits resolve synchronously; use `await Promise.resolve(null)` instead
The chunks are too large; the same await works once each chunk takes under 1 ms
await only yields inside an I/O callback; wrap the loop in fs.readFile so each await reaches the poll phase
items.explanation: Both prioritised queues drain to empty, so yielding to the microtask queue never lets timers or I/O run; setImmediate yields to the check phase.

items.prompt: After swapping native promises for a userland promise library in one module, two async chains that used to interleave now interleave one step differently, though both still finish correctly. What is the most likely mechanism?
items.answer: Awaiting a non-native thenable costs an extra microtask because the engine must wrap it, so that continuation resumes one tick later
distractors: Userland promises run their handlers as macrotasks, so they now wait behind every pending timer
The library resolves synchronously, so the awaiting function no longer yields at all
V8 drops the second await of any non-native promise, so one step of the chain is skipped
items.explanation: Native promises get a fast path (1 tick); a thenable costs one tick more. If two chains interleave 'wrongly', count ticks before assuming a bug.

items.prompt: A handler calls `sendAnalytics()` (an async function) without awaiting it, planning to attach `.catch(log)` inside a `setTimeout(..., 50)`. On Node 22 the call rejects. What happens?
items.answer: The process crashes with the error: rejections are checked at the end of the microtask checkpoint, and a catch attached in a later timer is too late
distractors: Node waits until the timer attaches the catch, then logs the error normally
The rejection is silently dropped, because nothing awaited the promise
Node prints a deprecation warning and keeps the process alive until the next GC
items.explanation: Since Node 15 the default is --unhandled-rejections=throw; attaching .catch later in the same tick is fine, in a setTimeout it is far too late. Fire and forget is fire and crash.

items.prompt: `setTimeout(log2, 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => setTimeout(log3, 0)); setTimeout(() => Promise.resolve().then(log4), 0);` prints 2 4 3. Why does 3 come last even though its .then ran before any timer?
items.answer: The .then only schedules a new timer, which joins the timers queue behind the two registered synchronously; a promise handler gives no priority to the work it queues
distractors: Timers created inside microtasks are clamped to 4 ms, so log3's timer is not due until after the others
The timers queue runs in reverse registration order when promises are involved, so the earliest one is last
log3's timer only runs after every pending microtask in the process has resolved, including log4's
items.explanation: Timers fire in the order they became due; track what each callback queues, not just when it runs.

items.prompt: A Node service stops responding and no timers fire. Which observation points at microtask/nextTick starvation rather than a deadlock?
items.answer: The process sits at 100% CPU while hung; a deadlock leaves the CPU idle
distractors: The heap grows steadily until the process is OOM-killed
The stack trace in a debugger shows two frames waiting on each other's lock
The process exits with code 0 after the last timer is cleared
items.explanation: Recursive nextTick, recursive Promise.then and a sync loop all look identical from outside: CPU pegged, responsive to nothing, timers never fire.

items.prompt: `button.addEventListener('click', cart.checkout)` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined" inside checkout (an ESM module), while `cart.checkout()` works. Why?
items.answer: this is decided at the call site; the listener calls the bare function with no dot, so implicit binding cannot apply and strict default binding gives undefined
distractors: Passing a method as an argument copies it, and the copy loses the properties stored on the cart
Event listeners always set this to the window object, which has no cart fields
checkout was defined in another module, and this always refers to the defining module's scope
items.explanation: this is part of the call, not the function. Moving the function where the dot did not follow drops from rule 3 (receiver) to rule 4 (default: undefined in strict/ESM). Fix with bind or an arrow wrapper.

items.prompt: `function P(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }` and `const P1 = P.bind({ ignored: true }, 1)`. What does `new P1(2)` produce, and why?
items.answer: A fresh object `{x: 1, y: 2}`: new outranks the bound receiver but keeps the bound arguments
distractors: The `{ ignored: true }` object mutated to hold x and y, because bind is permanent and wins over new
A TypeError, because bound functions cannot be used as constructors
A fresh object `{x: 2, y: undefined}`, because new discards both the receiver and the bound arguments
items.explanation: new is the highest-priority rule: it builds a new object as this even after bind, discarding the bound receiver while keeping bound arguments.

items.prompt: In an ESM file, `const counter = { n: 0, inc: () => this.n++ }` and `counter.inc()` throws. A callback `items.forEach(i => this.total += i)` inside a regular method works fine. What distinguishes the two?
items.answer: Arrows have no this of their own and resolve it lexically; the method's callback inherits the method's this, but an arrow used as the object method itself inherits module scope, which is undefined
distractors: Arrow functions bind this to the object literal only when called through forEach, so inc must be called via forEach too
Object literals freeze arrow properties, so `this.n++` fails while method shorthand is writable
counter.inc() passes counter as this, but arrows reject receivers that are plain objects
items.explanation: Arrows for callbacks, methods for methods: an arrow as an object-literal method has no enclosing method to inherit from, so this is module scope (undefined in ESM).

items.prompt: A base class has `static create(n) { return new Animal(n); }` and `class Dog extends Animal`. `Dog.create('Rex')` returns an object without Dog's methods. What change fixes it, and why does it work?
items.answer: Use `new this(n)`: inside a static method this is the class it was called on, so Dog.create builds a Dog
distractors: Redeclare create in every subclass, because static methods are not inherited through extends
Use `new super(n)`, because super in a static method points at the calling subclass
Use `Object.create(Animal.prototype)`, because new never runs subclass constructors from a static
items.explanation: extends wires the class-to-class chain too (Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal), so statics are inherited; hard-coding new Animal silently breaks every subclass.

items.front: A word counter does `counts[word] = (counts[word] || 0) + 1` with `const counts = {}` over user-submitted text. One document contains the word "toString". What does its count become?
items.back: 'function toString() { [native code] }1': the plain object inherits toString from Object.prototype, so the lookup is not undefined and + concatenates. No error, just a corrupt value downstream. Fix: Object.create(null), a Map, or Object.hasOwn checks.

items.front: A base class constructor calls `this.render()`; a subclass overrides render() and reads its own field `label = 'Save'`. On construction the button renders "undefined". Why?
items.back: Init order is base field, base constructor body, derived field, derived constructor body: the override runs before the subclass's fields are assigned. Fix: do not call overridable methods from a constructor, or pass the values as arguments.

items.front: An API endpoint accepts 5 MB JSON uploads and calls `JSON.parse` on them in the handler. Dashboards show p50 latency fine but p99 terrible across ALL endpoints. What is going on?
items.back: Each ~300 ms synchronous parse blocks the event loop, delaying every concurrent request, not just the upload. Fix: keep large CPU work off the JS thread (worker, streaming parser) or chunk and yield; watch it with monitorEventLoopDelay.

items.front: Legacy code sets `Dog.prototype = { bark() {} }` and a serializer later uses `obj.constructor.name` to tag records. Dog records are tagged "Object". Why?
items.back: constructor is an ordinary writable property on the prototype; replacing the prototype wholesale discards it, so lookup falls through to Object.prototype.constructor. Fix: add methods to the existing prototype (or use class), or restore constructor explicitly.
